title: SPSC Ring Buffer

statement.md: A single-producer single-consumer ring buffer has $c$ slots, indexed $0$ to $c-1$, and two indices: `head` (next slot to read) and `tail` (next slot to write). Both start at 0 and wrap around modulo $c$. To tell a full buffer from an empty one without a counter, **one slot is always left unused**: the buffer is empty when `head == tail` and full when `(tail + 1) mod c == head`. So it holds at most $c - 1$ items.

Simulate a stream of operations. `PUSH x` writes $x$ at `tail` and advances `tail` unless the buffer is full, in which case it prints `FULL` and changes nothing. `POP` reads at `head` and advances `head`, or prints `EMPTY` if the buffer is empty. A successful push prints `OK`; a successful pop prints the value read.

inputFormat: First line: $c$ and $t$. Then $t$ operations, one per line: `PUSH x` or `POP`.
outputFormat: One line per operation as described. After the last operation print `HEAD h TAIL t SIZE s` where $s$ is the number of items currently stored.
constraints: Operations are applied strictly in the given order

examples.input:
4 8
PUSH 1
PUSH 2
PUSH 3
PUSH 4
POP
PUSH 5
POP
POP
examples.output:
OK
OK
OK
FULL
1
OK
2
3
HEAD 3 TAIL 0 SIZE 1

hints: Do not track a size counter for the full test. Use the rule (tail + 1) % c == head.
The size is (tail - head + c) % c.

editorial.md: With one slot kept free, `head == tail` can only mean empty, so a producer and a consumer can each update only their own index. That is what makes the structure safe without locks: the producer writes `tail`, the consumer writes `head`, and each only reads the other.
The price is one wasted slot. A power-of-two capacity would let you replace `% c` with a bit mask, which is why production buffers usually use it. Here $c$ is arbitrary, so use the modulo.
